period: Museum opened 1 November 2025; collection c. 3100 BC to AD 400
summary: Over 100,000 objects, a six-storey staircase of kings and Tutankhamun's entire tomb in one building: here is how to take it on without wilting.
look: You come in through the atrium, a glass-roofed hall of about 10,000 square metres where the colossus of Ramesses II stands. Behind him the Grand Staircase climbs six storeys past more than 60 statues and sarcophagi to a terrace that looks out at the pyramids. The 12 main galleries, running in time order from prehistory to Roman Egypt, and the two Tutankhamun halls open off the upper level. The Khufu boats have a separate hall of their own.
story:
The old Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square opened in 1902 and was soon bursting, with objects stacked in basements and storerooms. A new museum beside the pyramids was first announced in 1992, and the design competition of 2002 drew 1,557 entries from 82 countries. A small Dublin practice, Heneghan Peng, won. Their building is a chamfered triangle whose north and south walls line up with the Great Pyramid and the Pyramid of Menkaure, about 2 kilometres away.

Then came the wait. Construction began in 2005, and the opening slipped again and again, for reasons ranging from funding to a pandemic. Trial visits began in October 2024, and the official opening came on 1 November 2025. The public returned on 4 November, the 103rd anniversary of the day Howard Carter's men found the first step of Tutankhamun's tomb.

The collection tops 100,000 objects, gathered from Tahrir, Luxor, Minya, Sohag, Alexandria and storerooms across Egypt, and at least 20,000 of them are shown for the first time. The main galleries run in four blocks: prehistory to the First Intermediate Period, the Middle Kingdom, the New Kingdom, and finally the last dynasties, when Greeks and Romans ruled. That last block is where your Ptolemies from Alexandria live.

How to tackle it: do not try to read everything. Climb the staircase slowly, because it is a free lesson in kingship. Do Tutankhamun while you are fresh; he needs at least 90 minutes. Use the period galleries for the pieces on your own list, and keep the Khufu boat for the end, when your feet hurt and all you want to do is stare. Plan on four hours, with a coffee in the middle.
details: From the atrium, look out through the glass front: the pyramids are visible from inside the building.
The main galleries run in time order: start at the oldest end and walk forward through 3,500 years.
The two Tutankhamun halls hold 5,398 objects; the crowds gather at the mask, the quiet cases are often the best.
The Khufu boat hall is separate: follow the signs and save some energy for it.
Take a coffee break halfway; in a museum this size, tired eyes stop seeing.
fun_fact: The 2002 design competition drew 1,557 entries from 82 countries, the second-largest architecture competition in history. The prize went to a small practice from Dublin.
narration: Welcome to the Grand Egyptian Museum. Take a breath, because this building holds more than 100,000 objects, and here is how not to drown in them. You are in the atrium, with Ramesses the Second towering ahead. Behind him rises the Grand Staircase, six storeys of kings, gods and stone coffins, ending at a terrace that looks straight at the pyramids, about 2 kilometres away. That is no accident. The architects lined up the museum's walls with the Great Pyramid and the Pyramid of Menkaure, so the whole building points at Giza. At the top are 12 main galleries, running in time order from prehistory to Roman Egypt, and two long halls given entirely to Tutankhamun: 5,398 objects from one small tomb, shown together for the first time. A separate hall holds Khufu's 4,600 year old cedar boat. My advice: climb the staircase slowly, because it tells the story of Egyptian kingship in stone. Then do Tutankhamun while you are fresh, and give him at least 90 minutes. Use the period galleries for the pieces you really want, and save the boat for last, when your feet hurt and you just want to stare. This museum was more than 20 years in the making and opened fully only in November 2025, so you are among its very first visitors. Right now, look out through the glass front of the atrium: on a clear day you can see the pyramids from inside.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, reign of Ramesses II, 1279-1213 BC
summary: An 11-metre Ramesses II who spent 51 years breathing traffic fumes in Ramses Square before moving into a calm hall under glass.
look: The red granite giant in the middle of the atrium is Ramesses II, 11 metres tall, standing in the classic striding pose with his left foot forward. Walk all the way round him: the scale only makes sense when you see people at his feet. Then step back towards the entrance for the full figure with the Grand Staircase behind.
story:
This colossus was carved more than 3,200 years ago for Ramesses II, who ruled Egypt for 66 years and put his name on more monuments than any other king. It stood at Memphis, the old capital just south of Cairo. In 1820 it was found at Mit Rahina, the village on the ruins of Memphis, broken into six pieces, and there it lay for decades.

In 1955 Gamal Abdel Nasser had the fragments brought to the square outside Cairo's main railway station. Early attempts to restore it where it lay had failed, so it was rebuilt in Cairo, held together with iron bars inside, and set on a 3-metre pedestal beside a fountain. The square was renamed Ramses Square, and for half a century the king watched over trains, buses and traffic jams.

By the 2000s the pollution and the vibration of traffic and metro were damaging the granite. Planning for a move began in 2002, and weeks before the real thing a replica was driven along the route as a rehearsal. On 25 August 2006 the statue, wrapped in rubber foam, travelled upright and in one piece on two flat-bed trucks to a temporary site near the pyramids. The trip took about ten hours. In 2018, after restoration, he made his last short move of about 400 metres into this atrium.

The museum says the hall is set so that sunlight reaches his face twice a year, around 21 February and 21 October, a nod to the sun festival of Abu Simbel.
details: Stand at his feet and look up: 11 metres is roughly a three-and-a-half-storey building.
Look at the feet: the left one strides forward, as in almost every standing Egyptian king.
Look for his names in cartouches; on Ramesside colossi they are often carved on the belt and upper arms.
Climb a few steps of the Grand Staircase and turn round for a higher view of his head.
fun_fact: Before the real statue crossed Cairo in 2006, engineers drove a full-size replica along the whole route, as a dress rehearsal for a granite king.
narration: In front of you stands Ramesses the Second, 11 metres of red granite, the king who ruled Egypt for 66 years. He was carved more than 3,200 years ago for Memphis, the old capital just south of Cairo. In 1820 he was found there, broken into six pieces, and he lay there for decades. Then in 1955 Gamal Abdel Nasser had him pieced together and stood up in the square outside Cairo's main railway station. The square was renamed Ramses Square, and for 51 years this king watched trains, buses and traffic jams, breathing exhaust and shaking every time the metro rumbled past. By the 2000s the pollution was eating the stone. So on 25 August 2006 he was wrapped in rubber foam and driven upright, in one piece, on two trucks to the desert near the pyramids. Engineers had already driven a full-size replica along the route, as a dress rehearsal. The trip took about ten hours. In 2018 he made his final short journey, about 400 metres, into this hall, and the rest of the museum grew up around him. The museum says sunlight reaches his face twice a year, around 21 February and 21 October, a little echo of Abu Simbel, which you will see on the 17th. Now walk right up to his feet and look at them: the left foot steps forward, as it does for nearly every Egyptian king, striding out into eternity.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, reign of Ramesses II, 1279-1213 BC
summary: The world's first 'hanging' obelisk: lifted on pillars so you can walk underneath and see the royal name on its base, hidden for over 3,000 years.
look: At the main gate on the plaza, a granite obelisk of Ramesses II stands on a steel structure carried by four massive pillars. Walk underneath and look straight up: the cartouche carved on its base, the face that always sat on a pedestal, is visible from below. Then step back to see the hieroglyphs running down its sides and the small pyramid at its tip.
story:
The obelisk comes from Tanis, in the north-eastern Nile Delta, where it lay on its side, broken in two. Tanis was the capital of the kings who ruled after the Ramesside age, from around 1070 BC, and they filled it with monuments brought from older sites, probably including Ramesses II's own Delta capital, Pi-Ramesses. So this stone had already travelled once before it came to Giza.

Restorers rejoined the two halves, and the builders of the museum added a twist. An obelisk normally stands on a base, so its bottom face is never seen. Here it is raised on a frame so visitors can walk beneath it and look up at the cartouche of Ramesses on the underside, out of sight for more than 3,000 years. Egyptian officials call it the world's first suspended obelisk.

To the Egyptians an obelisk was a ray of sunlight turned to stone, sacred to the sun god. Its pyramid-shaped tip, the pyramidion, was where the first light of dawn landed. Obelisks usually stood in pairs before temple gates. At Luxor Temple on the 22nd you will see one standing alone: its twin has been in the Place de la Concorde in Paris since the 1830s.
details: Stand directly underneath and look up for the cartouche, the oval ring around the king's name.
Look down the shaft for repeated cartouches: Usermaatre Setepenre and Ramesses Meryamun, his two main names.
See if you can spot where the two broken halves were rejoined.
Find the pyramidion at the tip, where the first rays of sunrise were meant to strike.
fun_fact: The word obelisk is Greek: obeliskos, a little roasting spit. Greek visitors to Egypt nicknamed these colossal needles after their kitchen skewers.
narration: Before you go inside, stand under the obelisk at the main gate. This granite needle was cut for Ramesses the Second, and it was found lying broken in two at Tanis, a royal city in the north-east of the Nile Delta. Later kings had brought it there from an older site, probably Ramesses' own capital, Pi-Ramesses. Restorers joined the halves, and then the museum did something new. Instead of planting it on a base, they raised it on a frame carried by four great pillars. Why? Because on its underside is a cartouche, the oval ring that holds the king's name, and nobody was ever supposed to see it. For more than 3,000 years it sat face down on a pedestal. Egyptian officials call this the world's first hanging obelisk. To an Egyptian, an obelisk was a frozen sunbeam, sacred to the sun god, and its little pyramid tip was where dawn struck first. And the word is Greek: obeliskos, a little roasting spit, a joke by Greek visitors about these giant stone skewers. Now walk underneath, tilt your head right back, and find the king's name above you.

period: Royal and religious sculpture from the Old Kingdom to the Roman period
summary: Six storeys of kings, gods and sarcophagi climbing towards a view of the pyramids: a crash course in what a pharaoh actually was.
look: The staircase rises six storeys from the atrium, with more than 60 large pieces on its steps and landings: royal statues, temple architecture, gods with kings, and stone coffins and sarcophagi. Climb slowly and meet the faces at eye level as you go. At the top, a terrace frames the pyramids of Giza.
story:
The pieces are grouped in four themes: the Royal Image, how a king wanted to be seen; Divine Houses, fragments of temples, the gods' homes on earth; Gods and Kings, the bond between them; and the Funerary section, sarcophagi heading for eternity.

The idea that ties it together is kingship. The pharaoh was not just a ruler. He was the son of the sun god and the living Horus, the one human being who stood between the gods and everyone else. Every temple ritual in Egypt was, in theory, performed by him. His job was to uphold maat, the order of the universe, against chaos, which in practice meant floods that came on time, enemies kept out and gods kept fed.

A royal statue was not a portrait in our sense. It was a body for the king's ka, his life force, a place where he could live on, receive offerings and keep doing his job forever. That is why the faces are calm and ageless, and why later kings happily recarved older statues with their own names. The statue was a role, not a likeness. Ramesses II was the champion recycler.

As you climb, watch the style move through the centuries. Old Kingdom kings are solid and serene. Middle Kingdom faces can look careworn, with heavy eyelids. New Kingdom kings soften into a faint smile and wear finely pleated linen. Ptolemaic statues often put Greek curls on an Egyptian body. And the climb ends at the pyramids: the newest museum framing the oldest monuments of kingship.
details: On each royal statue, look for the cartouche on the belt or back pillar: the name may not be the original owner's.
Try sorting the pieces into the four themes: Royal Image, Divine Houses, Gods and Kings, and Funerary.
Compare red granite, black granodiorite and yellow quartzite; much of the granite came from Aswan, your stop on the 18th.
Look for a king standing with a god at the same scale: that intimacy was the whole point of kingship.
At the top, turn round before the pyramid view: the staircase drops away below you like a hillside of statues.
fun_fact: Statues were recycled constantly. Ramesses II carved his name onto many older kings' statues, so the face above a Ramesses cartouche may belong to someone who died centuries before him.
narration: You are at the foot of the Grand Staircase, six storeys high, lined with more than 60 statues, temple pieces and stone coffins. Think of it as a staircase about one idea: what it meant to be a pharaoh. The king was not just a ruler. He was the son of the sun god and the living Horus on earth, the only person who could stand between the gods and humanity. Every ritual in every temple was, in theory, his job. His task was to keep maat, the order of the universe, and to hold back chaos. So his statues were not portraits as we know them. A statue was a body for the king's spirit, his ka, a place where he could live on and receive offerings forever. That is why the faces are calm and ageless, and why later kings happily carved their own names onto older statues: the statue was a job, not a likeness. The pieces here fall into four themes: the royal image, the houses of the gods, gods and kings together, and finally burial and the road to eternity. As you climb, watch the faces change over 3,000 years, from the serene kings of the pyramid age to the faint smiles of the New Kingdom. If you spot a Ptolemaic piece, look for Greek curls on an Egyptian body. And at the top, your reward: the pyramids, framed for you. Start now with the nearest king, and find the cartouche with his name on his belt or on the pillar behind him.

summary: The museum's final trick: climb six storeys of kings and the Giza pyramids appear, framed, about 2 kilometres away.
look: At the top of the Grand Staircase the building opens onto a view of the Giza plateau, where the pyramids stand on the desert edge about 2 kilometres away. On a clear day you can pick out the Great Pyramid of Khufu and its neighbours. Khafre's is the one with a pale cap of original casing near the top.
story:
The building was designed around this view. When Heneghan Peng won the competition in 2003, their idea was to tie the museum to the pyramids by lines of sight: the north and south walls of the building line up directly with the Great Pyramid of Khufu and the Pyramid of Menkaure. The whole museum, in a sense, points at Giza. It sits where the green Nile valley meets the desert plateau, the same kind of edge the pyramid builders chose.

So the long climb is deliberate. You walk up through 3,000 years of kings and gods, and the last thing you see is the first chapter: pyramids built about 4,500 years ago for Khufu, his son Khafre and Menkaure. Tomorrow, on the 12th, you will stand at their feet.
details: Find the Great Pyramid of Khufu, the largest; tomorrow you will be at its base.
Look for Khafre's pyramid by the pale cap near its summit: a patch of the smooth casing that once covered them all.
Notice the pyramids sit on the edge of the desert plateau, just above the green valley.
Take your photo, then turn round: the staircase falls away below you like a hillside of statues.
fun_fact: Khafre's pyramid often looks taller than his father's from a distance because it stands on higher ground and is steeper, but it is actually slightly smaller.
narration: You have climbed six storeys of kings and gods, and here is the reward: the pyramids of Giza, about 2 kilometres away, framed by the museum itself. This is no lucky accident. When the Dublin architects Heneghan Peng won the design competition in 2003, their big idea was to tie the building to these monuments by lines of sight. The museum's north and south walls line up with the Great Pyramid of Khufu and the Pyramid of Menkaure, so in a sense the entire building points at Giza. The climb tells a story: you walk up past statues made over 3,000 years, and you finish at the very first chapter, the pyramids built about 4,500 years ago for Khufu, his son Khafre and Menkaure. Tomorrow, on the 12th, you will stand at their feet. One trick for now: Khafre's pyramid often looks taller than his father's, because it stands on higher ground and is steeper, but it is actually a little smaller. Find it by the pale cap near its top, a patch of the original smooth casing that once covered them all.

period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, reign of Khufu, c. 2500 BC
summary: A 4,500-year-old cedar ship over 43 metres long, built for the king of the Great Pyramid and buried beside it as a kit of 1,224 pieces.
look: The ship fills its own long hall: 43.4 metres of mostly Lebanese cedar, 5.9 metres wide, with high curving ends and a cabin on deck. Walk the full length and watch how the planks curve up towards each end. The wood is original, not a replica.
story:
In 1954 the Egyptian archaeologist Kamal el-Mallakh was clearing debris along the south side of the Great Pyramid when he found a sealed pit carved into the bedrock. Inside lay a ship, taken apart into 1,224 pieces and laid out in a logical order, untouched since about 2500 BC.

Rebuilding it fell to Ahmed Youssef Moustafa, chief restorer of the Antiquities Department. Before touching a plank he studied tomb reliefs and models, and watched boatbuilders at work in Old Cairo, Maadi and Alexandria. The job took years. The hull is built shell-first, with no keel: planks bent and fitted edge to edge, joined with tenons, then lashed together with ropes of halfa grass. There is not a nail in it.

From 1982 the ship sat in a purpose-built museum beside the pyramid. In August 2021 it moved here, in one piece.

What was it for? Some see a solar barque, a ritual vessel to carry the resurrected king across the sky with the sun god Ra. Others think it was the funeral barge that brought Khufu's embalmed body from Memphis to Giza, or a ship he used for pilgrimages in life and then took with him. It shows some signs of having been in water, and it could probably float today. But it has no rigging for a sail and little room for rowers. The debate is open, and the museum's displays lay out the theories.
details: Look at the two ends: they curve up and finish like bundles of papyrus, a memory of Egypt's earliest reed boats.
Find the deck cabin, a small shelter for an important passenger, perhaps the king himself.
Look for the lashing holes along the timbers: the whole ship is tied together, not nailed.
Notice the wood: mostly cedar from Lebanon, shipped across the Mediterranean, the most prized timber in Egypt.
fun_fact: The ship came out of the ground as 1,224 pieces neatly stacked in order: a flat-pack kit 4,500 years old, without the instructions.
narration: You are looking at one of the oldest wooden ships ever found: over 43 metres of cedar from Lebanon, built for Khufu, the king of the Great Pyramid, about 4,500 years ago. In 1954 an Egyptian archaeologist, Kamal el-Mallakh, was clearing rubble along the south side of the pyramid when he found a pit cut into the rock and sealed with huge limestone blocks. Inside lay this ship, taken apart into 1,224 pieces and stacked in a sensible order, like a flat-pack kit without the instructions. Putting it back together fell to the chief restorer, Ahmed Youssef Moustafa. He studied ancient tomb pictures and models, and watched traditional boatbuilders at work, before he fitted a single plank. It took him years. The hull has no keel and no nails: the planks are fitted edge to edge and lashed together with ropes of grass. In 2021 the whole ship was moved here in one piece from its old museum beside the pyramid. What was it for? Some say it was a solar boat, to carry the dead king across the sky with the sun god. Others think it carried his body to Giza for the funeral, or that he sailed it on pilgrimages while he was alive. It shows some signs of having been in water, so it may well have floated once. Look now at the two ends of the ship: they curve up like bundles of papyrus, a memory of the reed boats of Egypt's first sailors.

period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, reign of Khufu, c. 2500 BC
summary: Khufu's second ship stayed sealed in its pit until 2011; Egyptian and Japanese restorers have been lifting and rebuilding it beam by beam.
look: This is the twin of the great ship, from a second pit found beside the first in 1954. Depending on how far the restoration has got, you will see conserved timbers, a partial reconstruction or work in progress. Compare its wood with the first boat's: it stayed underground far longer, and it shows.
story:
Two sealed boat pits were found on the south side of the Great Pyramid in 1954. The first was opened and its ship rebuilt. The second was left closed.

In 1987 Japanese researchers confirmed the second boat was still there, and a month later a team sponsored by the National Geographic Society drilled a hole about 10 centimetres wide through the cover slabs and lowered a small camera. The pictures showed the timbers lying in the dark. But the hole let air into the pit, and insects followed, damaging some of the beams.

The rescue was led by a team from Waseda University under Sakuji Yoshimura, working with Egyptian colleagues. In 2011 the cover stones of the pit were raised. From 2013 the beams were lifted one by one, treated in a laboratory set up on site, and taken to the Grand Egyptian Museum. By 2016 some 700 timbers had come out. Rebuilding a ship from wood this fragile is slow, and the museum presents the second boat among its newly restored pieces.
details: Compare the timbers with the first ship's: same king, same technique, very different state of preservation.
Look for the small holes along the planks where ropes passed: this ship was tied together too.
Look for any panels or film showing beams being lifted from the pit beside the Great Pyramid.
Tomorrow at Giza, look along the south side of the Great Pyramid, where both ships lay buried.
fun_fact: The 1987 camera survey was meant to be harmless, but the small drilled hole let air and insects into the sealed pit: proof that in archaeology, even looking can do damage.
narration: Next to the great ship lies its sibling, the second boat of Khufu. In 1954 archaeologists found two sealed pits on the south side of the Great Pyramid. They opened one: that is the ship you have just seen. The second they left closed. In 1987 a team sponsored by National Geographic drilled a hole about 10 centimetres wide through the cover stones and lowered in a camera. The pictures showed the timbers still lying in the dark. But the hole let air in, and insects followed and damaged some of the beams. The real rescue began with a Japanese team from Waseda University, led by Sakuji Yoshimura, working with Egyptian restorers. In 2011 they raised the cover stones, and from 2013 they lifted the beams one by one, treated each on site, and brought them here. Rebuilding a ship from wood this fragile takes years, so what you see depends on how far the work has got. Look closely at any reassembled section and find the small holes along the planks: just like its twin, this ship was tied together with rope, not nailed.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, burial c. 1323 BC; found 1922
summary: All 5,398 objects from Tutankhamun's small tomb, shown together for the first time since Carter emptied it. Here is how to read the halls.
look: Two long halls, about 7,000 square metres in all, hold the collection, with the gold mask as the centrepiece. The display follows the king himself: who he was, how he lived, then how he was buried and prepared for rebirth. Keep the tomb's four rooms in mind, Antechamber, Annexe, Burial Chamber and Treasury, and you can place almost every object.
story:
Tutankhamun came to the throne at eight or nine and died at about 19, around 1323 BC. Born Tutankhaten, he presided over the undoing of Akhenaten's religious revolution and the return of Amun and the old gods. His royal tomb was unfinished, so he was buried in a small tomb in the Valley of the Kings, now called KV62.

It was robbed twice within a few years of the funeral. Officials tidied up and resealed it, the entrance vanished under later rubble and workmen's huts, and that is why it survived. On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter's workmen uncovered a step. On 26 November Carter made a small breach in the inner doorway, held up a candle, and Lord Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything. 'Yes, wonderful things,' runs the famous version.

The tomb had four rooms. The Antechamber, about 7.9 by 3.6 metres, held 600 to 700 objects: beds, chariots, a throne, boxes of clothes. The smaller Annexe held more than 2,000: food, most of the shabtis, weapons, toys and games. The Burial Chamber was filled by four gilded shrines around the sarcophagus. The Treasury held the canopic shrine, the Anubis shrine, model boats and much of the jewellery. Carter's team numbered the finds from 1 to 620, adding letters for items within a group, and clearing the tomb took until November 1930; the last shipment reached Cairo in February 1932. The total: 5,398 objects.

For almost a century they were split between the Tahrir museum, storerooms and touring exhibitions. Here, for the first time, they are shown together. The mummy and the stone sarcophagus remain in the tomb, which you will visit on the 21st.
details: Picture the Antechamber: about 7.9 by 3.6 metres, smaller than many living rooms, yet it held 600 to 700 objects.
The Annexe, only 4.4 by 2.6 metres, held over 2,000 things: food, shabtis, weapons, toys. Look for those cases.
Carter numbered the finds 1 to 620 with letters for items in a group; you may spot these numbers on labels.
Follow the crowd to the mask, then go back to the quiet cases of linen, sandals and games, where the real boy is.
fun_fact: Carter's famous 'wonderful things' may be a polished memory: his journal entry for the day records a plainer 'Yes, it is wonderful'.
narration: You are entering the Tutankhamun galleries, and for the first time since Howard Carter emptied the tomb, the whole treasure is shown together: 5,398 objects from one small tomb. Tutankhamun became king at 8 or 9 and died at about 19, around 1323 BC. His grand royal tomb was not ready, so he was buried in a modest one in the Valley of the Kings, K V 62. Robbers broke in twice within a few years, officials tidied up and resealed it, and then rubble and workmen's huts buried the entrance. That is why it survived. On 4 November 1922 Carter's workmen found a step. On 26 November Carter made a small hole in the inner door and held up a candle, and Lord Carnarvon asked if he could see anything. Wonderful things, says the famous version. His diary is plainer: yes, it is wonderful. The tomb had four rooms. The Antechamber held 600 to 700 objects: beds, chariots, a throne. The tiny Annexe held over 2,000 more: food, shabtis, weapons and games. The Burial Chamber was filled by four golden shrines around the sarcophagus. And the Treasury held the canopic shrine, the Anubis jackal and the jewellery. Clearing it all took about ten years. Keep those four rooms in your head and you can place everything here. Now find his throne name in any cartouche: a sun disc, a scarab beetle, three little strokes and a basket. That spells Nebkheperure.

summary: Just over 10 kilos of gold, glass and stone: the face that became the face of ancient Egypt, with a protective spell written across its shoulders.
look: The mask is 54 centimetres tall and weighs 10.23 kilos, made of two layers of gold. On the brow rise the vulture Nekhbet, on your left, and the cobra Wadjet, on your right. The blue stripes on the nemes headcloth are coloured glass; the eyes are quartz with obsidian pupils, set in lapis lazuli. Walk behind it for the ten vertical and two horizontal lines of hieroglyphs on the back and shoulders.
story:
On 28 October 1925 Carter's team opened the innermost coffin and there it was, covering the king's head and shoulders. Carter's diary describes 'a golden mask of sad but tranquil expression'. The resins poured at the funeral had stuck it fast to the mummy, and it took heated tools to free it.

The gold is mainly 23-karat, alloyed with a little copper, which made it easier to hammer cold. A 2007 study found a thin surface layer that differs: about 18.4 karat on the face and neck and 22.5 elsewhere, which gives the face its paler tone. Inlays of lapis lazuli, carnelian, turquoise, amazonite, faience and glass complete it. The narrow beard, inlaid with blue glass to look plaited, weighs about 2.5 kilos.

That beard has had adventures. It was found detached in 1925 and fixed back with a wooden dowel in 1944. In August 2014 it came off while the mask was out of its case for cleaning, and was hastily glued back with epoxy, slightly off-centre. In 2015 a German-Egyptian team, with the conservator Christian Eckmann, removed the epoxy and reattached the beard with beeswax.

The spell on the back comes from chapter 151 of the Book of the Dead, a text used on masks since the Middle Kingdom. It identifies each part of the face with a god: 'Thy right eye is the night bark, thy left eye is the day bark.'

Was the mask made for him? Nicholas Reeves argues it was first made for Neferneferuaten, a female ruler just before him, citing the pierced ears and signs of altered cartouches. Eckmann, who has worked on the gold, sees no such alteration. The question is open.
details: Vulture on your left, cobra on your right: Nekhbet of Upper Egypt and Wadjet of Lower Egypt.
Look at the ears: they are pierced, one of the clues in the debate about who the mask was first made for.
The blue stripes on the headcloth are glass; the lapis lazuli is around the eyes and in the eyebrows.
Walk round the back for the Book of the Dead spell: ten vertical lines and two horizontal ones.
Check the beard: it sits straight now, fixed with beeswax since 2015.
fun_fact: When the beard came off in 2014 and was glued back with epoxy, the repair caused such a scandal that eight museum employees were disciplined in 2016.
narration: Here he is: the gold mask of Tutankhamun, probably the most famous face from the ancient world. It is 54 centimetres tall and weighs just over 10 kilos, two layers of gold hammered into shape. On 28 October 1925 Howard Carter opened the innermost coffin and found it resting on the king's head and shoulders. He wrote of a golden mask of sad but tranquil expression. Funeral resins had glued it to the mummy, and it took heated tools to free it. Look at the brow: a vulture on your left and a cobra on your right, the goddesses of Upper and Lower Egypt. The blue stripes of the headcloth are glass; the eyes are white quartz and black obsidian, rimmed in blue lapis lazuli. Now the beard. It was found loose, fixed back in 1944, and in 2014 it fell off during cleaning. Someone stuck it back with epoxy glue, a little crooked. A German and Egyptian team undid the damage in 2015 and reattached it with beeswax. One more puzzle: the ears are pierced, and some Egyptologists think the mask was first made for a female ruler, Neferneferuaten, and adapted for him. Others who have studied the gold closely disagree. Before you leave, walk round to the back and find the hieroglyphs on the shoulders: a spell from the Book of the Dead that turns each part of his face into part of a god.

summary: Three coffins nested like Russian dolls: two of gilded wood around an innermost one of solid gold weighing 110.4 kilos.
look: The three coffins show the king as Osiris, arms crossed over his chest holding the crook and flail, the vulture and cobra on his brow. The innermost, of solid gold inlaid with stones, is the smallest; the two outer ones are wood covered in gold and inlaid with coloured glass and semi-precious stones. Look at the feather pattern over the bodies: the wings of goddesses folded around the king.
story:
In the Burial Chamber, inside four gilded shrines, stood a quartzite sarcophagus carved with Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Selket, under a red granite lid painted yellow to match. Inside lay a gilded bier with lion heads and, on it, three human-shaped coffins, one inside another.

The two outer coffins are gilded wood inlaid with glass and stones. The innermost was the surprise: mainly solid gold, 110.4 kilos of it. When Carter's team reached it in 1925 it did not gleam. It was coated in black resin, poured over it during the funeral rites, which had hardened like pitch and glued coffin, mask and mummy together. The team tried warming the coffins in the sun and finally worked them apart with heated tools.

The face on the middle coffin looks different from the other two, and some Egyptologists think it was first made for someone else, perhaps a predecessor. Borrowing was common in this hurried burial.

Why this pose? The king is shown as Osiris, the god who was murdered, mummified and brought back to life to rule the dead. Crook and flail are Osiris's regalia; the vulture and cobra are the guardian goddesses of the two halves of Egypt.

Carter returned the mummy to the tomb in 1926, and it is still there in K V 62, with the stone sarcophagus. The outermost coffin stayed with it until July 2019, when it left the tomb for the first time for restoration at this museum.
details: Compare the three faces: the middle coffin's is often said to look like a different person.
On the gold coffin, look for Isis and Nephthys engraved with their wings spread across the lower body.
Find the crook and flail in the crossed hands, the regalia of Osiris.
Look at the brow for the vulture and the cobra, as on the gold mask.
Notice the feather pattern, called rishi, covering the bodies: protective wings wrapped round the king.
fun_fact: The gold coffin alone weighs 110.4 kilos, more than ten times the famous mask, and when it was found it was so coated in black resin that it hardly looked like gold at all.
narration: These are Tutankhamun's coffins, three of them, which fitted inside each other like Russian dolls. The two outer ones are carved wood covered in gold and inlaid with coloured glass and stones. The innermost is the shock: solid gold, weighing 110.4 kilos, more than ten times the famous mask. All three show the king as Osiris, the god who was killed, mummified and brought back to life. His arms cross over his chest holding the crook and the flail, and on his brow sit the vulture and the cobra, protectors of Upper and Lower Egypt. When Carter's team opened them in 1925, the gold coffin did not shine. It was coated in black resin, poured over it at the funeral, which had set hard like tar and glued coffin, mummy and mask together. They tried warming the coffins in the sun, and in the end they used heated tools. Some experts think the middle coffin was first made for someone else, because its face looks different. Compare the faces and decide for yourself. The mummy and the stone sarcophagus are still in the tomb, which you will visit on the 21st. The outermost coffin stayed there with them until 2019, when it came here for its first restoration. Now look at the body of the gold coffin and find the feathers: the wings of goddesses, wrapped around the king to protect him forever.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, early in the reign of Tutankhamun, c. 1330 BC
summary: A golden chair with a tender royal love scene under the rays of the banned sun god, and the king's name written both before and after the U-turn.
look: The throne is wood covered in gold and silver and inlaid with coloured glass, faience and stones. Lion legs support the seat with lion heads at the front, and the arms are winged cobras wearing the double crown. The famous scene is on the backrest: Queen Ankhesenamun touches her husband's shoulder with ointment while the Aten sun disc above sends down rays ending in little hands.
story:
Carter found it in the Antechamber, tucked under the hippopotamus-headed couch.

The backrest scene is pure Amarna art. The young king sits relaxed, one arm hooked over the back of his chair. His wife Ankhesenamun, a daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti, stands before him holding a small pot and touching his collar and shoulder with perfumed ointment. Above them shines the Aten, the sun disc that Akhenaten had made the one god, its rays ending in hands that hold out the sign of life. Private, tender moments like this almost never appear in royal art outside this short period.

The names give the date away. When the throne was made, the couple were Tutankhaten, 'living image of the Aten', and Ankhesenpaaten. In about the third year of his reign the court abandoned the Aten, restored Amun, and both names were changed to honour Amun instead. On this throne both versions of the king's name appear. It was either made during the transition or updated afterwards, and the Aten disc was simply left in place. One chair records a whole country's religious U-turn.
details: On the backrest, follow the Aten's rays down to the tiny hands, some holding the ankh, the sign of life.
Look at how the couple are built from inlays: coloured glass, stones and silver set into the gold.
Find the winged cobras forming the arms, each wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt.
Look for the lion heads at the front corners of the seat.
Hunt the cartouches: some name the Aten, others Amun. Both versions of his name are here.
fun_fact: The most famous couple portrait from ancient Egypt shows a teenage king having ointment rubbed on his shoulder by his wife. Royal art rarely got this domestic.
narration: This is Tutankhamun's golden throne, found by Howard Carter in the Antechamber, tucked under one of the great animal-headed couches. It is wood, sheathed in gold and silver and inlaid with coloured glass and stones. Lions' legs carry the seat, and the arms are winged cobras wearing the double crown. But the real treasure is the scene on the backrest. The young king lounges, one arm thrown over the back of his chair. His wife Ankhesenamun, daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti, leans towards him and touches his shoulder with perfumed ointment from a little pot. Above them shines the Aten, the sun disc that Akhenaten had made the one and only god, with its rays ending in tiny hands. This is Amarna art: intimate, relaxed, almost a family snapshot. And here is the clue to its date. The king was born Tutankhaten, living image of the Aten. In about the third year of his reign the court abandoned the Aten, brought back Amun, and he became Tutankhamun. On this throne both versions of his name appear, and nobody bothered to remove the Aten disc. One chair carries a whole country's religious U-turn. Look closely at the backrest now and follow the sun's rays down to the little hands, some of them holding out the ankh, the sign of life, to the royal couple.

summary: Four goddesses spread their arms around a gilded shrine that held the king's liver, lungs, stomach and intestines in four little gold coffins.
look: The tall gilded shrine stands on a sledge under a frieze of cobras, with a goddess on each side, arms spread in protection: Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Selket. Nearby is the chest carved from a single block of calcite, its four compartments closed by stoppers shaped like the king's head, and the four miniature gold coffins that held his organs.
story:
During mummification the embalmers removed the lungs, liver, stomach and intestines, dried them and stored them separately. The heart stayed in the body, because it would be weighed at the judgement of the dead. Each organ had a guardian, one of the Four Sons of Horus: human-headed Imsety for the liver, baboon-headed Hapy for the lungs, jackal-headed Duamutef for the stomach and falcon-headed Qebehsenuef for the intestines. Each was in turn protected by a goddess: Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Selket, the four you see here.

Carter found the shrine in the Treasury, against the east wall, with the Anubis jackal in front of it. Inside was the calcite chest, a single block of stone with four compartments. Each held a miniature coffin of gold inlaid with coloured glass and stones, a small copy of the king's own coffins, containing one organ.

Then the twist. Inside the little coffins, Egyptologists can read traces of another royal name beneath Tutankhamun's: Neferneferuaten, the mysterious ruler who came just before him. Much of his burial equipment seems to have been borrowed in a hurry.

The word 'canopic' is itself a mistake. Early Egyptologists linked such jars to Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus in Greek legend, who was said to be buried at Canopus in the Delta and worshipped there in the form of a jar.
details: Walk round the shrine: one goddess on each side. Selket is the one with the scorpion on her head.
Notice the goddesses' heads turn slightly to the side, a rare touch of movement in Egyptian sculpture.
In the calcite chest, find the four stoppers carved as the king's head in the nemes headcloth.
Look at the miniature gold coffins: each is a small copy of the king's own coffins.
fun_fact: The name 'canopic' comes from a Greek legend: Canopus, Menelaus' helmsman on the way home from Troy, was said to be buried near Alexandria and worshipped as a jar.
narration: In front of you is the shrine that guarded Tutankhamun's inner organs. During mummification, the embalmers took out the lungs, the liver, the stomach and the intestines, dried them, and stored them apart. The heart stayed inside the body, because it would be weighed at the judgement of the dead. Look at the four golden goddesses around the shrine: Isis, Nephthys, Neith, and Selket, the one with a scorpion on her head. Each stands on one side with arms spread to protect what is inside, and their heads turn slightly, a rare touch of life in Egyptian sculpture. Carter found this shrine in the Treasury, just behind the Anubis jackal. Inside was a chest carved from a single block of calcite, with four compartments sealed by stoppers in the shape of the king's head. And in each compartment, wrapped in linen, lay a tiny coffin of gold and coloured glass, a perfect copy of his big coffins, holding one organ. Now the twist. Inside those little coffins, experts can read traces of another name under his: Neferneferuaten, the mysterious ruler before him. Some of this equipment was borrowed. And a Greek footnote: the word canopic comes from Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus, said to be buried near Alexandria and worshipped as a jar. Look now at the stoppers of the calcite chest, and see the king's face, four times over.
